title: Avalokiteshvara
hook: the bodhisattva of compassion: Guanyin in China, Kannon in Japan, Chenrezig in Tibet

segments.voice: Yesterday, many Buddhas in countless worlds, and a toe touching the ground. Your line was countless worlds. Did you get a minute under the sky? Day one thousand one hundred five.

A bodhisattva has made a vow: not to rest until every being is free of suffering. So he works. He frees beings past counting. Then he stops and looks out over the world, and sees just as many still suffering as when he began. And in that moment of grief, as a Tibetan story tells it, his head splits apart. It's a startling place for a story about compassion to go. But it doesn't end there. Today, the bodhisattva of compassion: Avalokiteshvara, called Guanyin in China, Kannon in Japan, and Chenrezig in Tibet.
screen: `A VOW TO FREE EVERY BEING.` → `SO MANY STILL SUFFERING.` → `THE HEAD SPLITS APART.`

segments.voice: First, the remaking. In the Tibetan telling, the Buddha Amitabha, the bodhisattva's teacher, gathers up the pieces and makes them into many heads, so he can see suffering in every direction. Then his arms break too, from reaching for everyone, and Amitabha gives him many arms, and in the palm of each hand, an eye. That is the figure you may have seen in temples and on thangka paintings: heads rising like a crown, arms fanning out like a halo. Every part of that strange shape answers one question: how do you help when the need is this big? You see more widely, and you reach in more ways. Second, the names. The Sanskrit name was carried into many languages. In China it became Guanyin, a name usually given in English as the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In Japan, Kannon. In Tibet, Chenrezig. So the bodhisattva known in the story for many eyes is, by name, also the one who hears. Third, the forms. The Lotus Sutra says this bodhisattva takes whatever form will help the one in need: a monk, a king, a child, a woman. And over time the figure did change shape from land to land. In China, Guanyin came to be shown more and more as a woman robed in white. In Japan, Kannon stands at roadsides, in temples and on home altars. One bodhisattva, many faces, which is just what the sutra says to expect. Fourth, the honesty of the story. It admits that caring about suffering can break a person. The answer it gives isn't to care less. It's to be put back together with more eyes and more hands, and to keep going.
screen: `REMADE WITH MANY HEADS.` · `AN EYE IN EVERY PALM.` · `GUANYIN, KANNON, CHENREZIG.` · `WHATEVER FORM WILL HELP.` · then, large: `NOT LESS CARE. MORE HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Settle, and let the eyes close or rest low. For a little while, simply listen to the sounds around you, near ones and far ones. Then widen the listening. Bring to mind the people in your life, one at a time, and listen for what's underneath what they've been saying lately: a tiredness, a worry, a quiet ask they haven't quite made. You don't need to fix anything now. Just notice which one you heard. If it starts to feel heavy, come back to the breath and the sounds in the room. The bell holds the time.
Avalokiteshvara. The bodhisattva of compassion, Guanyin in China, Kannon in Japan, Chenrezig in Tibet: the one who sees, and hears, and reaches. Today's word.
Your line: the one who hears. Today, if you catch a quiet cry for help, even a small one, answer it with one thing you can actually do. Tomorrow, Manjushri. Day one thousand one hundred five.

howItsDone: Buddhists across East Asia and Tibet call on Avalokiteshvara by name in times of trouble; Tibetan Buddhists recite the mantra om mani padme hum, and temples in China and Japan keep images of Guanyin or Kannon, some with many arms.

fork.setup: you've vowed to free every being from suffering, and worked without rest. you look out and see as many suffering as when you began. what happens next, in the Tibetan story?
options: your head breaks from grief, and you're remade with more eyes and hands
you hand the vow to someone else
fork.reveal: the story lets the grief be real. then Amitabha remakes him to see in every direction and reach in more ways, and the vow goes on.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva of compassion, carried into Chinese as Guanyin.

notes: The shattered-head story is told as Tibetan tradition; traditional tellings give specific numbers (eleven heads, a thousand arms) that are left out under the claims rule. Confirm that it is Amitabha who remakes him and that the arms also break in the telling.
'Guanyin ... usually given in English as the one who perceives the sounds of the world': a rendering of the Chinese name (Guanshiyin), as on day 918; confirm.

Day 918 (year three) told the Lotus Sutra chapter and the hearing of cries; this day takes the shattered-head legend instead and touches the Lotus Sutra only for the forms. Day 268 named the Dalai Lamas as emanations, so that is not repeated.
howItsDone mentions om mani padme hum (taught on day 306) and says temples in China and Japan keep images, some many-armed.
